Greetings,


Two questions:

1) My impression of the examples was that the user reduce(k,vv) was called once per a key?  


2) Suppose that the map associates so many values to one key that in the reduce it is impossible to load them all into memory at once in the Reduce. Java gets around this with an iterable interface on values in the org.apache.hadoop.mapreduce.Reducer.reduce(key,values,context). How is it handled in RHadoop?



Thanks,
Jeremiah

On Tue, Aug 21, 2012 at 10:18 AM, jeremiah rounds <roundsj...@gmail.com> wrote:
Greetings,


Two questions:

1) My impression of the examples was that the user reduce(k,vv) was called once per a key?
Correct

2) Suppose that the map associates so many values to one key that in the reduce it is impossible to load them all into memory at once in the Reduce. Java gets around this with an iterable interface on values in the org.apache.hadoop.mapreduce.Reducer.reduce(key,values,context). How is it handled in RHadoop?

It is not. You need to use a larger key space or a combiner, that is avoid the problem with algorithm changes. While there is an iterator library in R the concept is not in very widespread use. This simplified or R-idomatic or whatever you want to call it reduce interface has been extremely well received by users and having control on the number of shuffle keys and distribution of data over those keys is any way good mapreduce programming practice (if I have one reducer take all the work, it doesn't help that it doesn't run out of memory if it doesn't terminate in a reasonable amount of time). I understand that it is a trade off and I haven't proven that one can always solve memory issues in the reduce phase by using a combiner or maybe an expanded key range and an additional job or in-memory post processing, but the experience so far has been generally positive and using combiners has other performance advantages and should be encouraged. It seems to me, again without any proof, that the only advantage of iterating through the values associated with a key in the reducer could be that one can apply more classical streaming algorithms (streaming not in the hadoop sense, in the theory of algorithms sense, that is when memory <<  input size) reading one value at a time. When using  a combiner, one has to work on whatever group of values is available on the map side, which can be large or small, create a summary or intermediate state of some sort and then combine those states on the reduce side. It is a more "lumpy" model of computation (see this for example) but I think it is very effective in mapreduce and  in many ways an emerging model. If you add to this that R performs best when using vectorized primitives and that it is a lot more complex, at least for the average R user, to write a stateful reducer, which is necessary with multiple reduce calls per key, the choice seemed pretty clear. I'd be happy to hear of use cases that support or negate this design choice and we may revisit it in the future, for instance providing an iterator interface. Thanks


Antonio





Thanks,
Jeremiah

I have a use case that consists of applying a classifier to a document-term-matrix (DTM) that is saved in a sparse format on HDFS. In this case the mapper is the identity function and the reducers actually do all the work, processing the data record-by-record. The reason for letting the reducers do all the work is that the DTM has to be sorted first (which happens automatically between the map phase and the reduce phase).

Based on my understanding, this cannot presently be implemented in rmr, even when using combiners.

Now, there is probably a way to rewrite the algorithm such that it also fits into the rmr-style framework, and this rewritten algorithm may or may not be contrived (I have not thought about this deeper). However, to me it seems that the approach in my paragraph above is a natural way of solving this problem.

By the way, I very much like the design of rmr's API in general. I'm just thinking that for some cases it might make sense to be able to write reducers in the usual Hadoop Streaming style (which is also the way RHIPE does it). Thanks.

On Wed, Sep 19, 2012 at 6:02 PM, Michael Smith <my.r...@gmail.com> wrote:
I have a use case that consists of applying a classifier to a document-term-matrix (DTM) that is saved in a sparse format on HDFS. In this case the mapper is the identity function and the reducers actually do all the work, processing the data record-by-record.

You are certainly aware that this is not a recommended mapreduce style, independent of the language or library used. You are foregoing any amount of locality by moving the complete dataset across the network.
The reason for letting the reducers do all the work is that the DTM has to be sorted first (which happens automatically between the map phase and the reduce phase).

I would like to understand better what you mean by sorted. The only way to achieve sorting in a conventional sense is to have a single reducer. I doubt this is what you are going for. Next best thing is  to have a custom partitioner that is order-sensitive, the standard adopted by terasort. We don't have custom partitioners in rmr but it is conceivable to add them. I don't have a third best thing.
Based on my understanding, this cannot presently be implemented in rmr, even when using combiners.
I was going to ask you why that would be the case, but I saw your next message.

Now, there is probably a way to rewrite the algorithm such that it also fits into the rmr-style framework, and this rewritten algorithm may or may not be contrived (I have not thought about this deeper). However, to me it seems that the approach in my paragraph above is a natural way of solving this problem.

I am not going to question the definition of "natural" but any mapreduce algorithm where the number of reducers is small is scalability challenged. Even if I gave you infinite memory, if you have only 5 or 50 different keys, that's as much parallelism as you'll ever get.
By the way, I very much like the design of rmr's API in general.
Thanks
I'm just thinking that for some cases it might make sense to be able to write reducers in the usual Hadoop Streaming style (which is also the way RHIPE does it). Thanks.

The java reduce calls handles one record at time, with sorting guarantees within the partition (if you use the default hash partitioner, you end up with a sorted random subset). The RHIPE reducer, the last time I checked, which admittedly was long ago, takes a subrange of records in this same order at a time, with no guarantee that all the records with the same key will appear in the same call. So it is not the same as Java, it is somewhere in between. At least that's my understanding and if I am wrong I would love to understand the current or correct way things are. Users making the switch from RHIPE have specifically complained about the work it takes to group all the same-key records. It is particularly hard because of the append bug which I had to work around. The streaming style makes sense in Java because it is a relatively efficient language, but with R the overhead of a single reduce call is such that you need to get some real work done in a single call, that's why the grouping was preferred. Sometimes with very large records this motivation is moot and sometimes with very small records and a large number of distinct keys the solution is not enough. So we would need not one or two but three reduce interfaces. We've done something like that on the map side for rmr 1.3 but the added complexity was significant. In 2.0 we are going to bring the complexity down again while keeping all (I hope) of the power gained in 1.3. How to do that in an elegant way on the reduce side is still unclear to me, but it's not a closed door and seeing potential use cases certainly helps.


Antonio

messages.subject: Re: [RHadoop:#259] Re: reduce(k,vv) what if vv is to large to fit in memory?
parts: I am very wary of adding new features. That's probably what make the design of rmr what it is. But this issue of the reducer is an important one. Would you sketch such an extended API for me?

Thanks for your insightful reply. Below is a rough sketch of what I have in mind. Of course for this particular example, the present rmr API is much better. The "alternative" API is just for illustration. The code below is inspired from the tweet count example in McCallum and Weston's book "Parallel R", page 92f.

## Current API.
mymap <- function(screenName, tweet)
  keyval(screenName, nchar(tweet))
myreduce <- function(screenName, vv) {
  tweetCount <- sum(unlist(vv))
  keyval(screenName, tweetCount)
}
mapreduce(input = input,
          map = mymap,
          reduce = myreduce)

## Alternative implementation of reducer API in the spirit of Hadoop
## Streaming, using the hypothetical 'get.next.value' function.
myreduce <- function(screenName) {
  tweetCount <- 0
  while (!is.null(reduce.value <- get.next.value(screenName))) {
    tweetCount <- tweetCount + reduce.value
  }
  keyval(screenName, tweetCount)
}
mapreduce(input = input,
          map = mymap,
          reduce = myreduce)

On Thursday, September 20, 2012 12:29:11 PM UTC+8, Antonio Piccolboni wrote:


On Wed, Sep 19, 2012 at 6:02 PM, Michael Smith <my.r...@gmail.com> wrote:
I have a use case that consists of applying a classifier to a document-term-matrix (DTM) that is saved in a sparse format on HDFS. In this case the mapper is the identity function and the reducers actually do all the work, processing the data record-by-record.

You are certainly aware that this is not a recommended mapreduce style, independent of the language or library used. You are foregoing any amount of locality by moving the complete dataset across the network.

 
The reason for letting the reducers do all the work is that the DTM has to be sorted first (which happens automatically between the map phase and the reduce phase).

I would like to understand better what you mean by sorted.

Say you have a whole bunch of records of the form (documentID, term, frequency). These records are not necessarily sorted according to documentID. Now, for each document, you want to calculate a table that shows how often a every term occurs in this document. For this, you need to first sort the records according to documentID, and then you can process the sorted records line-by-line, because you can be sure that once a new documentID appears, you have exhausted all the entries that belong to the previous documentID. This is an approach working directly with Hadoop Streaming (no R package required), and here I'm not sure how to do this without letting the reducers do all the work.

By the way, the reducers would have plenty of keys, since the number of keys is the same as the number of documents, which is large. So scalability in this sense is not a big issue, although you are right that it's not good mapreduce practice to move around all the data to the reducers.

And yes, this example would fit perfectly fine with the existing rmr API. I apologize for making such a strong statement about rmr earlier. The reason why I'm writing this post is to answer why in this use case the reducers do all the work and why it is necessary to sort the records. (I guess in rmr the sorting happens behind the scenes before calling the reducer.)

But this is a canonical combiner example! These are two anti-patterns in one example: don't use combiners in a reduce-heavy job and don't use R vectorized library functions when possible. Look just at the second one since I can cook up an example real quick

> system.time(sum(z))
   user  system elapsed 
  0.002   0.000   0.001 
> system.time({X = 0; for (x in z) X = X + x})
   user  system elapsed 
  0.517   0.004   0.524 

500 X slower!! Are you willing to wait 500 times longer or get hold of a cluster that's 500 times large (assuming linear scalability and assuming that it's feasible)? 

As far as getting warmed up to the combiner approach, people sometimes seem to think that combiners are only good for sums. This paper shows what can be done with several type of statistical summaries that can be assembled from summaries of subsamples with operations that are commutative and associative, that is compatible with combiners. Quantiles, heavy hitters, bloom filters, you name it. Highly recommended.


Antonio

But this is a canonical combiner example! These are two anti-patterns in one example: don't use combiners in a reduce-heavy job and don't use R vectorized library functions when possible. Look just at the second one since I can cook up an example real quick

Thanks for the paper, I'll take a look at it.

I know that using 'sum' is better in this case. That's why I wrote above that the example is only for illustration and that using rmr in this particular case would of course be better.

The reason why I wrote down this example of an API is because you asked for a suggestion of how to implement a reducer API that doesn't need to hold all of vv in memory. It is meant as an illustration of the API, not as an illustration of how to sum something up.

Anyway, thanks for your detailed replies and explanations.
